question: A 5-week-old exclusively breastfed male infant, who did not receive Vitamin K prophylaxis at birth, is brought with sudden onset of intracranial haemorrhage manifested as bulging fontanelle, seizures, and drowsiness. This is most consistent with which form of Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Early VKDB presents within 24 hours of birth and is almost always caused by maternal drug intake that interferes with Vitamin K (e.g., anticonvulsants, antituberculous drugs, warfarin). The presentation at 5 weeks of age excludes early VKDB.

Incorrect. Classic VKDB presents in the first week of life (days 2–7), typically as gastrointestinal bleeding, umbilical stump bleeding, or cutaneous bruising. It occurs in exclusively breastfed infants who did not receive prophylaxis. At 5 weeks of age, this presentation is beyond the classic window.

Correct! Late VKDB presents from 2 weeks to 6 months of age. It almost exclusively affects exclusively breastfed infants who did not receive Vitamin K prophylaxis. The hallmark is INTRACRANIAL HAEMORRHAGE in a previously well-appearing infant — which carries mortality and neurological sequelae rates of 30–50%. This is the catastrophic, preventable form of VKDB.

answers.text: Acquired prothrombin complex deficiency from hepatobiliary disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While cholestatic liver disease can cause Vitamin K deficiency bleeding (secondary VKDB), the scenario does not describe jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, or hepatomegaly. The clinical picture — exclusively breastfed, no Vitamin K prophylaxis, intracranial haemorrhage at 5 weeks — is the classic late VKDB presentation.

overallFeedback.feedback: VKDB timing: Early = <24h (maternal drugs). Classic = days 2–7 (GI/umbilical/skin bleeding). Late = 2 weeks–6 months (intracranial haemorrhage, exclusively breastfed, no prophylaxis). Age at presentation is the primary discriminator. Late VKDB = neurosurgical emergency + public health failure.

Excellent! Late VKDB (2 weeks–6 months) = exclusively breastfed + no Vitamin K prophylaxis + intracranial haemorrhage in a previously well infant. This is the most dangerous and preventable form. A single IM Vitamin K 1 mg at birth prevents all three forms.
